newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Solidarity mounts campaign to save shipyard.
newsitem.headline: Polish Solidarity mounts campaign to save shipyard.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity union launched nationwide protests on Wednesday to demand rescue for the collapsing Gdansk shipyard and reacted with fury when riot police expelled workers occupying government ministries.

"A horrible provocation" was how the rightist trade union's leader Marian Krzaklewski described a decision by the ex-communist-led government to send police to expel scores of workers from the economy, treasury and finance ministries.
Solidarity began the national action on Wednesday, after a receiver this month announced plans to wind up the Baltic coast shipyard where Solidarity arose in defiance of communism in 1980.

While 2,000 shipyard workers in Gdansk bricked up the door to offices of the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), which Solidarity accuses of letting the yard die, hundreds of workers occupied the ministries in the capital.

Police issued an ultimatum and then cleared the ministries, leading to scuffles at the treasury in which, union officials told PAP news agency, one worker was beaten unconscious and others slightly hurt. Witnesses said police were also injured.

"Once more the Red authorities are using force against a peaceful demonstration," protest leader Kazimierz Grajcarek told a news conference. He said union reinforcements were converging on the capital.

Krzaklewski told reporters Solidarity's national committee would meet on Thursday in Warsaw to decide a response. He said the union could in theory call a general strike if force was used against it, although it would try other options first.

Keeping up the pressure, Solidarity announced it would hold marches through Warsaw on Thursday and Friday in defence of the yard and against what it called police violence, while on Friday it would also organise protests in provincial capitals.
Solidarity's protest campaign aims to secure the rescue of the shipyard and help for other workers facing job losses in industries such as coal-mining in the southern Silesia region.
It is also stirring emotions before parliamentary elections due around September this year, by reviving divisions left from the struggle that led to the fall of communist rule in 1989.
The union has formed rightist parties into a powerful Solidarity Election Action (AWS), to take on the ex-communists sharing power in coalition with a Peasant party since 1993.
Both the union and the ex-communists accused each other of aggravating the shipyard issue for political gain, while the Peasants distanced themselves from the decision to use force.

"If the (protest) organisers have even a shred of a sense of responsibility for Poland, they will not play with its fate for their small political interests," SLD Prime Minister Cimoszewicz told reporters after a government meeting.
He said he would not allow the law to be broken with impunity.

Finance Minister Marek Belka, who blames bad management for the yard's plight, told a news conference there was a chance some jobs and plant could still be saved, apparently referring to proposals Cimoszewicz is to put to parliament on Thursday.
Gdansk radio reported this plan might involve the more successful Szczecin shipyard building ships in Gdansk for the Polska Zegluga Morska (PZM) merchant marine company.

The yard's receiver announced earlier this month he would dismiss its last 3,800 employees, and sell the assets piecemeal, after banks refused $100 million in credit to the shipyard to finance an order from a German shipowner.
